A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original LLM experiments on associative recall, parity, permutation tracking, and k-hop reasoning, including accuracy and computation-depth results.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F retain the original empirical results and add needle-in-a-haystack accuracy and computation-depth measurements.

M1.justification: The Transformer framework, recall protocol, Prefix Sum, Iterative Query, and existing task prompts are retained. The new benchmark applies existing protocols; the additional communication and voting formalizations develop their analysis rather than establish an implemented method change.

E1.justification: V2 adds long-document needle-in-a-haystack retrieval using Paul Graham essays, varying context length and needle position. This substantially extends the input environment beyond synthetic key-value recall. The original recall experiment moves to Appendix F.1; parity, permutation tracking, and k-hop coverage remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is retained in the corresponding experiments: Majority Voting versus CoA for recall, Majority Voting versus Iterative Query for k-hop reasoning, and the existing three-way state-tracking comparisons. Needle-in-a-haystack uses the existing recall comparator pair. Appendix H's theoretical voting model does not introduce a new empirical baseline.

E3.justification: The new needle experiment introduces a context-length and placement grid, Llama-8B evaluation, eight voters, 2,000-word CoA chunks, and tuning on a specified subset of the grid. Existing experiment settings are retained. The expanded 100/200/500-fact description documents k-hop conditions already represented in v1's figures.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds an analytical study of parity-error accumulation under independent node errors. Figure 3(c) adds recall computation-depth sensitivity to chunk size. Appendix E newly reports voting-count and task-specific tuning analyses, although their outcomes are mostly summarized rather than presented as full ablation curves.

E5.justification: Appendix E.5 specifies ten repetitions and mean accuracy for the new needle experiment. The existing 100-run, seed-42 prescription and standard-error displays remain. No new formal significance-testing procedure is documented; the added phrase 'no significant improvement' alone does not establish one.

E6.justification: Figure 3 adds needle-retrieval accuracy grids and approximately constant CoA computation-depth results across chunk sizes. For example, at 100,000 words and 50% needle depth, CoA scores 1.00 versus Majority Voting's 0.00. Newly reported tuning findings include little benefit beyond eight voters. Original experimental curves are retained; these are additional results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: V2 adds the parity-tree error formula and proof in Lemma D.1, a formal majority-voting definition and super-polynomial separation proof in Appendix H, and a fixed-precision soft-attention simulation proposition and proof in Appendix I. Appendix G also develops the argument for representing multi-token messages as sequential token transmissions.

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contributions remain substantially unchanged, but Section 6 adds a stronger, quantified central claim. Proposition 6.1 states that exact parity at logarithmic depth requires 2^{Ω(N^c)} majority-voting agents, whereas Prefix Sum uses N agents. V1 discussed advantages over voting without this depth-matched separation claim.

C2.justification: Appendix D explains how persistent independent errors can drive parity accuracy toward chance as problem size grows. Appendix H explicitly restricts the voting separation to zero-error computation and leaves approximate computation open. Appendix I specifies finite precision, finite width, and bounded absolute positional encodings for transferring lower bounds.

D1.justification: V2 discloses additional tuning ranges for voting, parity, permutations, and k-hop reasoning. It also documents the needle query and answer, essay-corpus repetition, selected configurations, and tuning subset. Existing prompts and code-access information remain; these disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: V2 adds Aspnes et al. (1991), Kamradt (2024), Jerad et al. (2025b), and Li and Cotterell (2025), while removing Bhattamishra et al. (2020). Appendix H sharpens the comparison with Mirtaheri et al. by contrasting their setting with depth-matched communicating protocols. The broader research positioning is retained.

P1.justification: The recall presentation and parts of Appendix B are rewritten, Section 6 is expanded, and the original recall discussion moves to Appendix F.1. Experimental appendices are renumbered around new sections, with scattered wording and bibliographic capitalization edits. Most existing prose and the main section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds a three-panel needle figure, relocates v1's recall bar chart as Figure 6, and reflows existing appendix plots. The summary table and other experimental displays are retained. Figure 1(b)'s final inter-agent message changes from 1 to 0, introducing an inconsistency with the sender's displayed parity of 1.

improvement.justification: The depth-matched voting separation and proof substantially strengthen a central comparison that v1 treated largely qualitatively. The error-propagation analysis and explicit transfer conditions improve understanding of the theory's practical limits, while the long-document experiment and tuning disclosures strengthen empirical support. These gains retain the original evidence and outweigh the small new Figure 1(b) inconsistency. The voting theorem remains restricted to exact computation, and the new retrieval evaluation is narrow.
